enrichment.short_title: CPS v Bate: in charge and section 5(2) Road Traffic Act 1988
key_facts: The respondent was found not guilty by Birmingham magistrates of being in charge of a motor vehicle with excess alcohol after drinking at a pub and returning to his parked Ford Focus.
He sat in the driver's seat with keys but the engine off; his intention was to collect a disabled parking sticker and arrange a taxi home via his wife.
The justices held the prosecution had failed to prove he intended to take or assert control, and dismissed the information without reaching the statutory defence.
The prosecutor appealed by case stated under DPP v Watkins guidance on 'in charge'.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' acquittal on a section 5(1)(b) drink-driving charge.
enrichment.outcome: Both questions answered in the negative; the justices' decision was quashed and the case remitted to a different bench for rehearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where the defendant is owner and sitting in the vehicle with keys, he is prima facie in charge; lack of intention to drive is relevant only to the section 5(2) defence on the balance of probabilities, not an ingredient the prosecution must prove to the criminal standard.
legal_issues: Whether the justices correctly applied DPP v Watkins on being 'in charge'
Whether intention to drive was wrongly treated as part of the prosecution case
Whether the statutory defence under section 5(2) should have been considered

enrichment.short_title: Timmins v Conn: IVA supervisor and onerous property exclusion
key_facts: Roger Fogg's creditors approved an IVA supervised by Stephen Conn; the matrimonial home at 24 Hunters Field was modified into the arrangement after initially being excluded.
A NatWest second charge later eliminated equity; the supervisor treated the property as excluded under clause 6.2.3 without formally exercising that power.
Mr Fogg remortgaged and used released funds to pay voluntary contributions while the supervisor completed the IVA as successful.
Creditor Mr Timmins applied under section 263(3) after Fogg was removed as a party to the proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Chancery judge's refusal to set aside completion of an individual voluntary arrangement and exclusion of the debtor's home share.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the section 263 application against the supervisor alone was misconceived once relief against the debtor was abandoned.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 6.2.3 of an IVA does not empower a supervisor unilaterally to release property originally brought into the arrangement; exclusion required variation under paragraph 17.1 with debtor and creditor consent, and no valid exclusion occurred here.
legal_issues: Construction of 'onerous property' in IVA clause 6.2.3
Whether the supervisor validly excluded the debtor's half share in the home
Whether declarations or compensation could be granted without the debtor as party
Whether the IVA had completed successfully

enrichment.short_title: Jemma Trust v KBL: permission to cross-appeal on tax counsel advice
key_facts: Etherton J held Kippax Beaumont Lewis negligent over a 1997 assent vesting the Hulton Land Fund and rejected claims that tax counsel had expressly advised executing the assent.

enrichment.short_title: SCT v Trafigura: fuel oil blending contracts and repudiatory breach
key_facts: South Caribbean Trading agreed to sell 484,000 barrels of fuel oil to Trafigura under contract 5536 linked to companion contracts for wet fuel oil blendstock and cutter.
SCT sought to deliver bought-in conforming fuel oil rather than product blended exclusively from Trafigura-supplied components.
Trafigura refused delivery in March 2001; SCT claimed to accept that refusal as repudiation after demanding confirmation by a deadline.
Moore-Bick J ordered trial of preliminary issues on delivery source, delivery dates, extension and acceptance of repudiation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court determination of preliminary issues on liability in a fuel oil sale dispute.
enrichment.outcome: On agreed assumptions, SCT could not deliver bought-in fuel oil under contract 5536; delivery time was varied to June 2001; Trafigura repudiated and SCT validly accepted that repudiation under Glencore principles.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 8 priced fuel oil by reference to cutter and blendstock actually used in the delivered blend, so contract 5536 required delivery of product blended from components supplied under contract 5508-2 unless Trafigura consented otherwise; contractual correspondence could vary delivery dates and a deadline-bearing notice could still accept repudiation.
legal_issues: Whether SCT was obliged to deliver fuel oil derived only from contract 5508-2 components
Whether the delivery date was varied or extended to June 2001
Whether Trafigura repudiated by refusing bought-in delivery
Whether SCT effectively accepted repudiation by its 23 March 2001 communications

enrichment.short_title: Technocrats v Fredic: Mareva security and charge over solicitor-held funds
key_facts: Technocrats claimed commission on Hampton Court House after Field J held Fredic must accept a qualifying £7m offer; Fredic refused and was sued.
A freezing order required £700,000 security; by consent GSC Solicitors held that sum pending further order when the injunction was discharged.
Fredic entered administration in November 2004 while Technocrats pursued summary judgment and argued it had a preferential charge over the held money.
The dispute turned on whether standard freezing-order 'security' language created proprietary rights in an insolvency.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Queen's Bench hearing on permission for insolvency administration proceedings, summary judgment, and the status of funds held under a consent discharge of a freezing order.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment refused; Technocrats had no security interest in the £700,000; GSC to pay the money to the administrator subject to an undertaking on further dealings.
enrichment.ratio: Standard Mareva security provisions and consent undertakings protect against dissipation of assets in personam and do not make the claimant a secured creditor with priority in administration unless the order obliges satisfaction of any judgment from the fund, following Cretanor and Flightline.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 16 security in a freezing order creates a charge
Whether consent solicitor-held funds gave Technocrats priority over the administrator
Whether permission should be granted for summary judgment during administration
Whether further freezing relief against individual defendants remained appropriate

enrichment.short_title: R v Marcus: unsafe convictions after unmasked video identification
key_facts: Marcus was convicted of seven knifepoint cash-machine robberies and one false imprisonment after a trial before Judge McCreath.
Police used masked then unmasked video identification compilations after failing to find eight sufficiently similar volunteers for the suspect's age and grey beard.
The unmasked procedure was adopted without proper notice, contrary to Code D, and Inspector Hunt accepted it was blatantly unfair.
The trial judge admitted the evidence as a case-specific transparency solution, but the Court of Appeal condemned the evasion of the Code.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal against convictions relying on video identification evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; convictions quashed on counts 4, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17; convictions on counts 8 and 10 upheld on independent DNA and identification evidence.
enrichment.ratio: A deliberate post-hoc unmasked video identification procedure that necessarily violates Code D must be excluded; unsafe convictions result where the flawed identification was essential, but unaffected counts supported by strong independent evidence need not be quashed.
legal_issues: Admissibility of unmasked video identification after failed masked procedure
Whether Code D violations rendered convictions unsafe
Whether remaining convictions were contaminated by the flawed procedure

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref No 113/2004: lenient sentence for hammer robbery of elderly couple
key_facts: Dean Follows pleaded guilty to robbery, two Valium supply offences and possessing a lock-knife in a public place.
He struck a 69-year-old man repeatedly with a claw hammer in the victims' home after a spontaneous confrontation over tobacco, causing skull fractures.
He grabbed the elderly partner's handbag and left substantial blood injuries and psychological harm; he confessed shortly after arrest.
The Crown Court sentenced him to five years for robbery concurrent with six months on the other counts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 alleging an unduly lenient custodial sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted but the court declined to increase the sentence; five years was lenient but not unduly lenient given the guilty plea, remorse, drug rehabilitation and double jeopardy.
enrichment.ratio: Even where residential robbery of vulnerable elderly victims with a weapon warrants a much higher starting point after trial, a substantial discount for guilty plea, genuine remorse and double jeopardy may justify leaving a lenient but not unduly lenient sentence undisturbed.
legal_issues: Appropriate custodial starting point for spontaneous home robbery with a hammer
Effect of guilty plea and remorse on sentence level
Whether double jeopardy should prevent increase on reference

enrichment.short_title: R (Anton) v SSHD: asylum removal, wardship and family jurisdiction limits
key_facts: The Anton family from Sri Lanka faced removal after the father's asylum appeal failed; wardship was commenced over Robinson Anton shortly before a scheduled flight.
Mrs Bollen, whose son was Robinson's close friend, sought residence orders and argued family proceedings were not a device to frustrate removal.
The Home Office pursued removal while family proceedings continued and did not disclose pending removal directions when a hearing was vacated in September 2004.
Munby J sat simultaneously in judicial review and family proceedings concerning overlapping relief.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Concurrent family wardship/residence proceedings and judicial review of removal directions with interim injunctive relief.
enrichment.outcome: Family proceedings were not to be summarily dismissed and should proceed urgently to trial; judicial review permission applications were adjourned; Bodey J's wardship-based restraint was discharged and interim relief extended pending permission decisions; IND non-disclosure was strongly criticised.
enrichment.ratio: Family courts cannot by wardship or section 8 orders restrain the Secretary of State's immigration removal powers, but genuine welfare disputes may proceed while immigration decisions remain subject to separate public-law review; fairness requires disclosure of removal directions when adjournment of related proceedings is under discussion.
legal_issues: Whether family proceedings were an abuse of process to delay removal
Whether wardship could restrain removal of an immigration-controlled child
Lawfulness of removal directions while family and JR proceedings were pending
Whether the IND unfairly withheld notice of removal directions from parties

enrichment.short_title: Kent CC v HSE: PUWER guard availability on post-hole borer appeal

statutes_considered.title: Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998

key_facts: Kent County Council was convicted of failing to prevent access to dangerous machinery after employee Jack Lane was injured by an unguarded PTO shaft on a post-hole borer.
The auger had been supplied with a guard but none was fitted or available at the depot when the equipment left for the site.
The council had issued training and a memorandum requiring guarded PTO use, but magistrates found no guard was available prior to the accident.
The council applied to remit the case stated to annex evidence challenging those factual findings.

enrichment.outcome: Application refused; case stated withdrawn; council ordered to pay HSE costs subject to assessment.
enrichment.ratio: On regulation 11 the employer must provide effective measures to prevent access to dangerous parts; a finding that no PTO guard was available at the depot at the material time was open to magistrates and defeats the prosecution case even if employees also breached instructions.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates were entitled to find no guard was available at the depot
Whether the correct test was guard availability rather than onsite fitting
Whether employee dereliction prevented the availability finding

enrichment.short_title: Render v Whitrod: permission appeal on historical Australian abuse claim
key_facts: Mrs Render, originally from Germany, claimed she was abducted and raped by Australian Commonwealth Police Commissioner Raymond Whitrod in the 1960s.
She alleged forced abortion of twins, deportation from Australia and prior unsuccessful proceedings on the same allegations.
Judge Walton struck out the claim as having no reasonable grounds and as an abuse of process; permission to appeal was refused.
She renewed the application orally in the Court of Appeal, arguing Crown employment made the claim justiciable in England.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against strike-out of tort claims relating to events in Australia.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; even if any claim existed it could only be pursued in Australia and the English proceedings were an abuse of process.
enrichment.ratio: Alleged crimes and assaults committed in Australia by an Australian public official are not justiciable in English courts merely because the defendant is said to be a Crown employee; stale foreign tort claims with no supporting evidence and prior litigation are properly struck out as abusive.
legal_issues: Whether English courts had jurisdiction over 1960s events in Australia
Whether the claim had any reasonable prospect of success
Whether the proceedings were an abuse of process
